lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- How Does She Compare
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Viviane Rodrigues de Oliveira | Lesson 6 -- How Does She Compare

listenings.text: Last year I had two offers on the table and I chose the smaller company. Everybody told me I was wrong. The other one was bigger, the salary was about fifteen per cent higher, and the office was nicer. So why did I say no? Three reasons. First, the manager. In the second interview the manager of the smaller company asked me better questions. She wanted to know what I was bad at. Nobody asks that. Second, the career path was clearer. They showed me a real document, with real steps, and the bigger company only said we will see in a year. And third, the commute is shorter, which sounds small until you add it up. Forty minutes a day, every day. Money is easier to compare than everything else, so people compare the money and forget the rest. I did the opposite, and one year later I am still happy.

There is one question that comes up in every process, on both sides of the table. Why you and not them. When I am hiring, the candidate asks me. When I am the candidate, they ask me. And the worst answer is always the same: the one where everything is perfect. We are more flexible, we pay better, we grow faster, our culture is stronger. Nobody believes it, because no company is better at everything. The answer that works has three parts. One thing where you are clearly better, with a number if you have one. One thing where you are honestly worse. And then the sentence that ties it together: so if what matters most to you is money, they are the better choice, and if it is stability, we are. That last sentence sounds like you are losing the argument. You are not. You are the only person in the room who sounds true.

extra_audio.text: We are more flexible than most retail companies. Our career path is clearer, because we published it. Our store turnover is eleven points lower than the sector average. Their bonus is bigger than ours, and that is true.

paras: This report compares four retail groups. Our group is the second largest by workforce, with about six hundred people. The largest one has almost twice our size, but it is not the most attractive employer in the sector.

On money, we are behind. Our average salary is a little lower than the sector average, and the bonus of our biggest competitor is bigger than ours. Their bonus is also harder to reach, because it depends on the result of the whole company and not on the store.

On everything else, we are ahead. We are more flexible than the other three: two of them still ask for five days at the office and we are hybrid. Our career path is clearer, because we published it last year. And our store turnover is eleven points lower than the sector average, which is the number the board looks at.

The honest conclusion is simple. We are not the company that pays the most. We are the company that keeps its people the longest, and after the certification our reputation is stronger than our salary.
